title: Clone Graph
problem: You get a reference to one node of a connected undirected graph. Each node has an integer val and a list of neighbors. Return a deep copy of the graph: every node must be a new object, and the copies must be connected in exactly the same way as the originals.
example: Explanation: 4 nodes in a square 1-2-3-4-1. The output has the same shape, but every node is a brand-new
intuition: Copying one node is easy: new Node(val). The hard part is the neighbour list. When you copy node 1 you need the copy of node 2, and when you copy node 2 you need the copy of node 1 again. If you just recurse blindly you loop forever (1 → 2 → 1 → 2...), and you would also create two different copies of the same node.

The fix is one hash map: original → copy. Before you create a copy, check the map. If the copy exists, reuse it. If it does not, create it, put it in the map immediately, and only then go fill its neighbours. Putting it in the map before recursing is what breaks the cycle: when node 2 asks for node 1's copy, the map already has it. The map also acts as the "visited" set, so every node and every edge is handled once.
notes: Say it like this: "The only trick is avoiding infinite loops and duplicate copies, so I keep a map from original node to its copy. I could do it in two BFS passes (create all copies, then wire them), but a single DFS works: create the copy, put it in the map before recursing, then clone each neighbour. Both are O(V + E) time and O(V) space."
Edge cases: null input; a single node with no neighbours; a self-loop (node in its own neighbour list) works because the map is filled before recursing.
Common mistakes: Putting the copy in the map after the loop (infinite recursion); comparing by val instead of by reference when values may repeat; returning the original node somewhere by accident.

Follow-ups: "Graph is huge, recursion may overflow?" Use the BFS version with an explicit queue. "Graph is disconnected?" Then you would be given all nodes; run the same clone from every node not yet in the map. 10.2
simple: Make a full copy of a graph: new nodes with the same connections.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Do the job in two separate passes so each pass is simple.
steps: BFS over the original graph. For every new node you discover, create its copy (no neighbours yet) and store original → copy.
Loop over every entry in the map and fill the copy's neighbour list by looking up the copy of each original neighbour.
Return the copy of the starting node.
approaches.why: Each pass touches every node and every edge once; the map and queue hold up to V entries. (Any correct clone must read every edge, so there is no asymptotically slower "real" brute force. This version just does two traversals instead of one.)
approaches.simple: First visit every node and make an empty copy of each, then go around again to connect the copies.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: One DFS that creates and wires in the same pass.
steps: If the node is already in the map, return its copy.
Otherwise create the copy and put it in the map before visiting neighbours.
For each neighbour, recursively clone it and append the result to the copy's neighbour list.
approaches.why: Every node is cloned once and every edge is followed once (twice for undirected, still O(E)); the map plus recursion stack are O(V).
approaches.simple: Depth-first: copy a node, store it in a map, then copy its neighbours. The map stops you from copying a node twice and handles loops.

title: Course Schedule
pattern: Topological sort / Cycle detection in directed graph
problem: There are numCourses courses labelled 0 to numCourses - 1. prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take b before a. Return true if you can finish all courses, otherwise false.
example: Explanation: 0 needs 1 and 1 needs 0: a cycle.
intuition: Draw an edge b → a for each pair ("b unlocks a"). You can finish everything exactly when this directed graph has no cycle. A cycle means a group of courses all waiting on each other.

The cleanest way to check this is Kahn's algorithm. Count, for every course, how many prerequisites it still needs (its in-degree). Courses with in-degree 0 can be taken right now, so put them in a queue. When you "take" a course, every course it unlocks loses one needed prerequisite; if that drops to 0, it becomes takeable. If at the end you took all numCourses, there was no cycle. Courses on a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they are never taken.
Trace for [[1,0],[0,1]]: in-degree of 0 is 1, of 1 is 1. The queue starts empty, we take 0 courses, 0 ≠ 2, so false.
notes: Say it like this: "This is cycle detection in a directed graph. Brute force runs a fresh DFS cycle check from every course, O(V·(V+E)). Optimal is Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take courses with zero remaining prerequisites; if I manage to take all of them there is no cycle. That is O(V + E) time and space. A 3-colour DFS with a shared state array is equally fast."
Edge cases: No prerequisites (always true); a self-loop [0,0] (in-degree never hits 0, correctly false); duplicate pairs (in-degree counted twice and decremented twice, still correct).

Common mistakes: Reversing the edge direction (it still works for detecting cycles, but breaks Course Schedule II's order); using a plain visited boolean for directed cycle detection (it flags a node reached by two different paths as a cycle, which is wrong).
Follow-ups: "Return an order" is Course Schedule II (next question). "Minimum number of semesters" = run Kahn level by level and count levels. 10.3
simple: Courses have prerequisites. Can you finish them all, or is there a circular requirement?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Check, from every course separately, whether a cycle can be reached.
steps: Build the adjacency list b → a.
For each course s, run a fresh DFS with a 3-state array (0 = unvisited, 1 = on current path, 2 = finished).
If the DFS ever steps onto a node that is "on current path", there is a cycle: return false.
If no start finds a cycle, return true.
approaches.why: Each of the V starts runs a full DFS from scratch because the state array is reset; space is the graph plus the state array and recursion stack.
approaches.simple: From each course, run a search looking for a path that comes back to itself.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees).
steps: Build the adjacency list b → a and indeg[a]++ for each pair.
Push every course with in-degree 0 into a queue.
Pop a course, count it as taken, and decrement the in-degree of every course it unlocks; push any that reach
Return taken == numCourses.
approaches.why: Each course enters the queue at most once and each edge is relaxed once; adjacency list plus in-degree array and queue.
approaches.simple: Kahn's method: start with courses that need nothing, take them, and unlock courses whose prerequisites are now done. If you take every course, there's no cycle.

title: Course Schedule II
problem: Same setup as Course Schedule: numCourses courses and pairs [a, b] meaning b must come before a. Return any valid order in which to take all courses. If it is impossible, return an empty array.
example: Explanation: 0 first, then 1 and 2 (any order), then 3. [0,2,1,3] is also accepted.
intuition: A valid order is exactly a topological order of the graph b → a: every edge points forward in the list. Kahn's algorithm builds one naturally: the order in which courses come out of the queue is a valid order, because a course enters the queue only after all its prerequisites have been popped.
If a cycle exists, some courses never reach in-degree 0, so the produced order is shorter than numCourses. That is the signal to return [].
notes: Say it like this: "A valid order is a topological sort. Brute force repeatedly scans for a course whose prerequisites are all done, O(V·(V+E)). Kahn's algorithm does it in O(V + E): queue the zero in-degree courses, pop them into the answer and unlock their dependents. If fewer than numCourses come out, there is a cycle and I return an empty array."
Edge cases: No prerequisites (any permutation, e.g. 0..n-1); a cycle (return []); isolated courses (in-degree 0 from the start).
Common mistakes: Edge direction: for [a, b] the edge is b → a (b first). Getting it backwards gives the reversed order. Forgetting the length check, which returns a partial order when a cycle exists.

Follow-ups: "Lexicographically smallest order?" Replace the queue with a min-heap (O((V+E) log V)). "DFS version?" Push a node onto a stack after all its descendants finish, then reverse; needs 3-colour states to detect cycles. 10.4
simple: Give an order to take all the courses, respecting prerequisites.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Simulate semesters by repeated scanning.
steps: Keep taken[] and the list of prerequisites for each course.
Repeatedly scan all courses; pick any untaken course whose prerequisites are all taken, append it to the order.
If a full scan picks nothing and courses remain, there is a cycle: return [].
approaches.why: Up to V rounds, and each round re-checks every course and all of its prerequisites.
approaches.simple: Keep scanning for a course whose prerequisites are all taken, take it, and repeat.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Kahn's algorithm, recording the pop order.
steps: Build b → a adjacency and in-degrees.
Queue all in-degree-0 courses.
Pop a course, append it to the answer, decrement its neighbours, push any that hit
If the answer has numCourses entries return it, else return [].
approaches.why: Every course is pushed/popped once and every edge is relaxed once.
approaches.simple: Kahn's method with a queue: the order you take courses out of the queue is the answer.

title: Graph Valid Tree
problem: You have n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges. Return true if these edges form a valid tree: all nodes are connected and there are no cycles.
intuition: A tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges. That single fact removes half the work: - If edges.length!= n - 1, it cannot be a tree. - If it has exactly n - 1 edges, then "connected" and "acyclic" are equivalent. So you only need to check one of them.

Union-Find checks "no cycle" very naturally: process edges one by one; if both endpoints already have the same root, this edge closes a cycle. With n - 1 edges and no cycle, the graph is automatically connected.
notes: Say it like this: "A tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges, so I check that first; then I only need to rule out a cycle. Brute force does a BFS before adding each edge, O(E·(V+E)). With Union-Find each edge is nearly O(1): if both ends already share a root it is a cycle. Total about O(V + E) time and O(V) space."
Edge cases: n = 1, edges = [] is a tree (true); n = 2, edges = [] is not (false, caught by the count check); duplicate edges (caught as a cycle).
Common mistakes: Checking only "no cycle" without the edge count (a forest passes); checking only the edge count (a cycle plus an isolated node passes).
Follow-ups: "Do it with DFS?" Check count, DFS from 0, return visitedCount == n. "Edges stream in?" Union- Find handles that online. 10.5
simple: Do these edges form a tree (connected, no cycles)?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Add edges one at a time and search the graph each time.
steps: If edges.length!= n - 1, return false.
For each edge (u, v): run a DFS/BFS on the edges added so far to see if v is already reachable from u. If yes, this edge makes a cycle: return false. Otherwise add it.
If all edges were added, return true (n − 1 edges, no cycle ⇒ connected).
approaches.why: One full graph search per edge; adjacency list plus visited array.
approaches.simple: A tree has exactly n − 1 edges. For each new edge, check whether its two ends were already connected.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Edge count check + Union-Find.
steps: If edges.length!= n - 1, return false.
Initialise parent[i] = i.
For each edge, find both roots (with path compression). Same root ⇒ cycle ⇒ false. Otherwise union them.
Return true.
approaches.why: α is the inverse Ackermann function (≤ 4 in practice) thanks to path compression and union by size; only the parent/size arrays are stored.
approaches.simple: Union-Find: join the ends of each edge; if they already share a leader, the edge would make a cycle.

title: Max Area of Island
problem: You get an m x n binary grid where 1 is land and 0 is water. An island is a group of 1 s connected horizontally or vertically. The area of an island is its number of cells. Return the largest island area, or 0 if there is no land.
example: Explanation: Cells (0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,1) form one island of size 5; (3,3) is an island of size 1.
intuition: Treat the grid as a graph: each land cell is a node with up to 4 land neighbours. An island is a connected component, and its area is the component size.

So scan the grid; whenever you find land you haven't visited, flood-fill from it and count how many cells you reach. To avoid revisiting, "sink" each visited land cell by setting it to 0. Every cell is then visited at most once overall, not once per island.
notes: Say it like this: "Each island is a connected component, and the area is its size. Brute force BFSes from every land cell with a fresh visited set, O((mn)²). Instead I DFS once per island and sink cells as I count them, so every cell is visited once: O(mn) time, O(mn) worst-case stack."
Edge cases: All water (return 0); whole grid is land (area m·n, deep recursion); single cell grid.
Common mistakes: Marking visited after recursing (double counting); counting diagonal neighbours (not allowed here).

Follow-ups: "Don't modify the input?" Use a separate boolean[][] visited. "Stack overflow on 1000x1000?" Use iterative BFS/stack. "Max area if you may flip one 0 to 1?" That is LC 827: label islands with ids and sizes, then for each 0 sum the distinct neighbouring island sizes + 1. Number of Connected 10.6
simple: Find the biggest island of 1s in the grid.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Measure the island of every land cell independently.
steps: For every land cell, run a BFS with a brand-new visited array and count the cells reached.
Track the maximum.
approaches.why: Up to m·n starts, each BFS can cover the whole grid; the visited array is m·n.
approaches.simple: From every land cell, flood out with a fresh visited grid and count.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: DFS that sinks land as it counts.
steps: Scan every cell. When you see a 1, call dfs(r, c).
dfs returns 0 if out of bounds or water; otherwise sets the cell to 0 and returns 1 + dfs of its 4 neighbours.
Keep the maximum returned value.
approaches.why: Each cell becomes 0 the first time it is visited, so it is processed once; recursion depth can reach m·n in the worst case (a snake- shaped island).
approaches.simple: Scan the grid; when you hit land, flood it with DFS, counting cells and sinking them so they aren't counted again.

title: Number of Connected Components In An Undirected Graph
problem: You have n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges. Return the number of connected components.
intuition: Start by assuming every node is its own component, so the answer is n. Every edge that joins two different components merges them, so the count drops by exactly 1. An edge inside an already-joined component changes nothing.

That is exactly what Union-Find gives you: union(a, b) returns whether a merge happened, and you decrement the count when it does. A DFS works too: count how many times you have to start a new DFS from an unvisited node.
notes: Say it like this: "Start with n components; every edge that joins two different components reduces the count by one. A naive label-propagation is O(V·E). DFS from each unvisited node is O(V + E) with an adjacency list. Union- Find does it in about O(V + E) time but only O(V) extra space, and it works for streaming edges."
Edge cases: No edges (answer n); duplicate edges; self-loops (find gives the same root, ignored).
Common mistakes: Decrementing on every edge instead of only on successful merges; forgetting path compression (can degrade to O(V) per find).
Follow-ups: "Size of the largest component?" Track size[root]. "Edges deleted over time?" Process deletions in reverse as additions (offline trick). 10.7
simple: How many separate groups does this graph have?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Label propagation.
steps: Give each node a label equal to its own index.
Repeat: for every edge, set both endpoints' labels to the smaller of the two. Stop when a full pass changes nothing.
Count distinct labels.
approaches.why: The minimum label can need up to V passes to travel across a long path, and each pass scans all E edges.
approaches.simple: Give each node its own label and keep copying the smaller label across edges until nothing changes.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: DFS over an adjacency list.
steps: Build the adjacency list.
For each unvisited node, increment the count and DFS to mark its whole component.
approaches.why: Every node and edge is visited once, but you have to store the full adjacency list and a recursion stack.
approaches.simple: For each unvisited node, start a search that marks its whole group, and count the searches.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Union-Find with a running count.
steps: count = n, parent[i] = i.
For each edge, find both roots. If they differ, union them and count--.
Return count.
approaches.why: Near-constant time per edge with path compression + union by size, and no adjacency list is built: only the parent and size arrays. It also works if edges arrive as a stream.
approaches.simple: Union-Find: start with n groups and subtract one every time an edge joins two different groups.

title: Number of Islands
problem: Given an m x n grid of characters '1' (land) and '0' (water), return the number of islands. An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically, surrounded by water. Everything outside the grid is water.
intuition: This is "count connected components" on a grid. Scan cells in order. The first time you hit an unvisited '1', you have found a new island: add 1, and then flood-fill (DFS) the whole island so none of its other cells are counted again. When the scan finishes, the counter is the number of islands. The flood fill marks visited cells by overwriting '1' with '0'. That is why each cell is processed only once in total.
notes: Say it like this: "Islands are connected components of land cells. A naive approach BFSes from every land cell, O((mn)²). Instead I scan once; each time I hit unvisited land I count an island and flood-fill it to water, so every cell is processed once: O(mn) time, O(mn) worst-case recursion. BFS or Union-Find give the same complexity."
Edge cases: Empty grid / all water (0); all land (1); a single long snake island (deep recursion).
Common mistakes: Comparing char to int 1 instead of '1'; counting diagonals; forgetting bounds checks before reading the cell.

Follow-ups: "Can't modify the grid?" Use a visited matrix. "Recursion limit?" BFS with a queue. "Cells turn into land one by one, report count after each?" That is Number of Islands II: Union-Find, add a new component per land cell and union with land neighbours. 10.8
simple: Count islands of 1s in a grid (up/down/left/right connections).

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Count an island only at its "representative" cell.
steps: For every land cell, BFS its island with a fresh visited array and find the smallest index r*n + c in that island.
If the current cell is that smallest cell, count it.
approaches.why: A full BFS per land cell; each BFS can touch every cell.
approaches.simple: Flood each land cell's island with a fresh visited grid and count each island once.

approaches.lead: DFS flood fill that sinks the island.
steps: Scan every cell.
On a '1': count++, then DFS from it, turning every reachable '1' into '0'.
Return count.
approaches.why: Every cell is sunk at most once; worst-case recursion depth is m·n when the whole grid is one winding island.
approaches.simple: Scan the grid; every time you find land, count it and sink the whole island with DFS.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problem: An m x n island has height heights[r][c] at each cell. The Pacific touches the top and left edges; the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges. Rain water flows from a cell to a 4-directional neighbour whose height is less than or equal to the current height. Return all cells from which water can reach both oceans.
intuition: The direct question ("from this cell, can water get to both oceans?") needs one search per cell. Flip it around: start from the oceans and walk uphill. If water can flow from cell A down to cell B, then from B you can "climb" back to A (neighbour height ≥ current height).

So run one search from all Pacific border cells, climbing to neighbours that are at least as high: everything reached can drain to the Pacific. Do the same from the Atlantic border. The answer is the intersection of the two reached sets. Two searches over the grid instead of m·n searches.
notes: Say it like this: "Simulating rain from every cell costs O((mn)²). I reverse the direction: from each ocean's border I DFS uphill, marking every cell that can drain to that ocean. Two searches, then I intersect: O(mn) time and space."
Edge cases: Single row or column (every cell touches both oceans); all heights equal (every cell qualifies); corners belong to both oceans (top-right and bottom-left).
Common mistakes: Using > instead of >= when climbing (equal heights do allow flow); using one shared visited grid for both oceans.
Follow-ups: "BFS instead?" Same idea with two multi-source queues. "Only one ocean?" One search is enough. 10.9
simple: Water flows to equal or lower cells. Which cells can reach both oceans?

approaches.lead: Simulate water from every cell. 1. For each cell, DFS downhill (to neighbours with height ≤ current), with a fresh visited array. 2. Record whether the search touches the top/left edge (Pacific) and the bottom/right edge (Atlantic).
steps: If both, add the cell to the answer.
approaches.why: One full grid search per cell.
approaches.simple: From every cell, search to see if it can reach the Pacific and the Atlantic.

approaches.lead: Reverse DFS from both coastlines.
steps: pac[][], atl[][] boolean grids.
DFS from every top-row and left- column cell into pac, from every bottom-row and right-column cell into atl. Move only to neighbours with height ≥ current (climbing).
Collect cells where both are true.
approaches.why: Each of the two searches marks each cell at most once; two boolean grids plus recursion stack.
approaches.simple: Flip the direction: climb uphill from each ocean's border. Cells reached from both sides are the answer.

title: Redundant Connection
problem: A tree with n nodes (labelled 1..n) had one extra edge added, so edges has n edges and exactly one cycle. Return an edge you can remove so the result is a tree. If several answers exist, return the one that appears last in the input.
example: Explanation: 1-2-3-1 is a cycle; [2,3] is the last edge of it in the input.
intuition: Add edges one by one. Before adding (u, v), ask: "are u and v already connected?" If yes, this edge closes the cycle, and it is the answer. Why is it the last cycle edge in the input? Because the cycle can only close when its final edge arrives; every other cycle edge came earlier.
"Are they already connected, then connect them" is exactly what Union-Find answers in near O(1).
notes: Say it like this: "Process edges in order; the first edge whose endpoints are already connected closes the only cycle, and it is automatically the last cycle edge in the input. Checking connectivity with DFS each time is O(n²); with Union-Find it is O(n·α(n)), basically linear, with O(n) space."
Edge cases: Nodes are 1-indexed, so size arrays n + 1; the cycle may involve the very first edges (answer is still the edge that closes it).

title: Rotting Oranges
problem: In an m x n grid, 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange, 2 is a rotten orange. Every minute, each fresh orange that is 4- directionally next to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if that is impossible.
intuition: Rot spreads from all rotten oranges at the same time, one step per minute. That is BFS with many starting points: put every initially rotten orange in the queue at "minute 0". Process the queue level by level; each level is one minute, and it rots the fresh neighbours of the current level.

The time when a fresh orange rots equals its BFS distance to the nearest rotten orange, and multi-source BFS computes exactly that. The answer is the number of levels needed to rot everything. If some fresh orange is never reached (walled off by empty cells), return -1.
notes: Say it like this: "Rot spreads from all rotten oranges simultaneously, so it's a multi-source BFS where each level is a minute. Simulating the grid minute by minute is O((mn)²); BFS processes each cell once for O(mn) time and space. I stop when no fresh oranges remain and return -1 if some are unreachable."
Edge cases: No fresh oranges at all (answer 0, even with no rotten ones); fresh but no rotten (−1); fresh isolated by empty cells (−1).

Common mistakes: Running a separate BFS per rotten orange (gives wrong times and is slower); incrementing minutes once too many (loop on q non-empty without the fresh > 0 guard, then subtract 1 inconsistently); marking cells rotten when dequeued instead of when enqueued (duplicates in queue).
Follow-ups: "Return the time each orange rots?" Store the BFS level in a distance matrix. "Diagonal spread too?" Use 8 directions. 10.11

steps: Each minute, scan the whole grid and collect every fresh orange that has a rotten neighbour.
Rot all of them at once (collect first, then rot, so rot doesn't spread twice in one minute).
If nothing changed, stop. Answer is the minutes passed if no fresh remain, else -1.
approaches.why: Up to m·n minutes (a long winding chain), and each minute scans all m·n cells.
approaches.simple: Each minute, scan the whole grid and rot fresh oranges next to rotten ones.

title: Surrounded Regions
problem: Given an m x n board of 'X' and 'O', capture every region of 'O' s that is completely surrounded by 'X' by flipping those 'O' s to 'X'. An 'O' region that touches the border (directly or through connected 'O' s) is not captured. Modify the board in place.
example: Explanation: The bottom 'O' is on the border, so it stays. The middle region is surrounded and gets flipped.
intuition: Deciding "is this region surrounded?" is awkward. The opposite question is easy: which 'O' s are safe? Exactly those connected to a border 'O'.

So: DFS from every 'O' on the border and mark everything it reaches as safe (temporarily '#'). Then sweep the board: any remaining 'O' was not reachable from the border, so it is captured → 'X'. Every '#' goes back to 'O'. This "start from the boundary" trick is the same reverse thinking as Pacific Atlantic.
notes: Say it like this: "Instead of checking whether each region is surrounded, I find the safe 'O's: anything connected to a border 'O'. I DFS from the border marking them, then flip every remaining 'O' to 'X' and restore the marked ones. That is O(mn) time and space versus O((mn)²) for checking each cell separately."
Edge cases: Board with 1 or 2 rows/columns (every cell is on the border, nothing flips); all 'O'; all 'X'.
Common mistakes: Flipping during the brute-force scan (changes later checks); forgetting to restore '#' back to 'O'; starting DFS only from corners instead of the whole border.

Follow-ups: "Union-Find version?" Union border 'O's to a virtual node, union adjacent 'O's, then flip any 'O' not connected to the virtual node. "Stack overflow?" Use BFS from all border 'O's at once. 10.12
simple: Capture every O region that is completely surrounded by X.

If not, remember this cell to flip.
After checking all cells, flip the remembered ones.

title: Walls And Gates
problem: An m x n grid rooms has three values: -1 (wall), 0 (gate), and INF = 2147483647 (empty room). Fill each empty room with the distance (number of 4-directional steps) to its nearest gate. If a room cannot reach any gate, leave it as INF. Modify in place.
intuition: "Distance to the nearest of many sources" is the textbook case for multi-source BFS, just like Rotting Oranges. Put all gates in the queue at distance 0 and run one BFS. BFS reaches cells in order of distance, so the first time a room is reached is from its nearest gate. Because a room is filled only once (while it is still INF), every cell is processed once.
Doing one BFS per gate also works, but rooms get processed once per gate.
notes: Say it like this: "Running a BFS from each gate costs O(gates · mn). Multi-source BFS seeds the queue with every gate at distance 0; BFS expands in distance order, so the first time a room is reached is from its nearest gate. Each room is filled once: O(mn) time and space."
Edge cases: No gates (everything stays INF); rooms enclosed by walls (stay INF); grid with only walls.
Common mistakes: BFS from each room to find a gate (even slower); checking rooms > 0 instead of == INF in the optimal version (would overwrite already-correct distances).
Follow-ups: "Return distance to nearest gate only for one query room?" Single-source BFS from that room. "Weighted steps?" Use Dijkstra with all gates as sources. 10.13

title: Word Ladder
pattern: BFS on implicit graph (shortest path, unweighted)
problem: Given beginWord, endWord and a dictionary wordList, find the length of the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in wordList. The length counts words, including both ends. Return 0 if no sequence exists. (beginWord need not be in the list; endWord must be.)
example: Explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog (5 words).
intuition: Think of each word as a node, with an edge between two words that differ in exactly one letter. "Shortest sequence" in an unweighted graph means BFS.

The question is how to find a word's neighbours quickly. Comparing it with every word in the dictionary costs O(N·L) per word. Instead, generate candidates: for each of the L positions try all 26 letters, and check each candidate in a hash set. That is 26·L lookups per word, independent of N. Remove a word from the set when you enqueue it so it is never visited twice.
notes: Say it like this: "Words are nodes and one-letter differences are edges, so the shortest sequence is a BFS. Comparing against every word to find neighbours is O(N²·L). Generating the 26·L one-letter variants and checking them in a hash set makes it O(N·L²·26). I delete words from the set when I enqueue them so each is visited once."
Edge cases: endWord not in the list (0 immediately); beginWord == endWord (not possible per constraints, but would be 1); beginWord present in the list (remove it so you don't revisit).

Common mistakes: Marking visited when dequeuing instead of enqueuing (huge duplicate queues, TLE); returning steps instead of steps + 1 when the generated word is endWord; forgetting to restore the character after the inner loop.

Follow-ups: "Faster?" Bidirectional BFS: expand the smaller frontier from both ends, often a big constant-factor win. "Return all shortest sequences?" Word Ladder II: BFS to build a parent map level by level, then backtrack from endWord. 10.14
simple: Change one letter at a time, using only dictionary words, to go from start to end. How many words in the shortest chain?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: BFS where neighbours are found by scanning the whole list.
steps: BFS from beginWord, storing (word, length).
To expand a word, loop over every unvisited word in the list and check whether they differ in exactly one position.
Return the length when endWord is popped; 0 if the queue empties.
approaches.why: Each of the N words, when expanded, is compared against all N words at O(L) per comparison.
approaches.simple: BFS where, to find neighbours, you compare against every word in the list.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: BFS with generated neighbours and a hash set.
steps: Put wordList into a set. If endWord is not in it, return 0.
BFS level by level from beginWord, steps = 1.
For each word, for each position, try 'a'..'z'; if the new word is endWord, return steps + 1; if it is in the set, remove it and enqueue it.
approaches.why: Each word is dequeued once; it builds 26·L candidate strings, each costing O(L) to create and hash. The set and queue store up to N words of length L.
approaches.simple: BFS where neighbours are found by trying all 26 letters at each position and checking the word set.

title: Flood fill algorithm
problem: Given an image as an m x n grid of integers, a starting pixel (sr, sc) and a new color, recolor the starting pixel and every pixel 4-directionally connected to it that has the same original color. Return the modified image. (LeetCode 733.)
example: Explanation: All 1s connected to the centre become 2. The bottom-right 1 is not connected (diagonal does not
intuition: This is the "paint bucket" tool. Remember the original color at (sr, sc), then DFS: recolor the current pixel and spread to neighbours that still have the original color. Recoloring is the visited marker: once a pixel has the new color it no longer matches the original, so it won't be visited again.
One trap: if color equals the original color, recoloring changes nothing, so pixels never stop "matching" and the DFS loops forever. Return immediately in that case.

Common mistakes: Missing the same-color guard (stack overflow); reading image[sr][sc] after it is already painted (original color lost).

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Repeated sweeps until nothing changes.
steps: Keep a boolean filled[][], set filled[sr][sc] = true.
Repeatedly scan the whole grid: any unfilled pixel with the original color that has a filled neighbour becomes filled. Stop when a scan changes nothing.
Paint every filled pixel with color.

approaches.simple: Keep scanning the grid, spreading the fill one ring at a time until nothing changes.

approaches.lead: Single DFS from the start pixel.
steps: orig = image[sr][sc]. If orig == color, return the image unchanged.
DFS: if out of bounds or pixel ≠ orig, stop; else paint it and recurse on 4 neighbours.
approaches.why: Each pixel is painted at most once; recursion depth up to m·n.
approaches.simple: DFS from the start pixel, recolouring every neighbour with the original colour.

title: Number of islands (8 directions)
problem: Given an n x m grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count the islands, where land cells are connected in all 8 directions (horizontal, vertical and diagonal). This is the GFG / Striver version of Number of Islands. (GFG's newer version uses 'L' / 'W' instead of '1' / '0'; only the characters change.)
example: Explanation: (0,1) touches (1,0) diagonally, so all land is one island.
intuition: Identical to 10.7 except for the neighbour list: instead of 4 directions you check 8. The easiest way to write that is two loops dr in {-1,0,1}, dc in {-1,0,1}, skipping (0,0).

Edge cases: Diagonal-only connections (they merge islands here); all water; single cell.
Common mistakes: Keeping only 4 directions out of habit; forgetting that (dr, dc) = (0, 0) is the cell itself (harmless here because it is already visited, but be aware).

approaches.why: A full BFS per land cell.

title: Distance of nearest cell having one
problem: Given an n x m binary grid, return a grid of the same size where each cell holds the distance to the nearest cell containing 1. Distance is |r1 - r2| + |c1 - c2| (moves in 4 directions). Assume at least one 1 exists. (GFG version; LeetCode 542 "01 Matrix" is the same problem measuring distance to the nearest 0.)
intuition: Same shape as Walls and Gates: many sources (all the 1 s), and we want each cell's distance to the nearest one. Seed a BFS queue with every 1 at distance 0. BFS then visits cells in increasing order of distance, so the first time a cell is reached, its distance is final.
Without obstacles, the BFS step distance equals the Manhattan distance, which is what the problem asks for.
notes: Say it like this: "Comparing every cell with every 1 is O((nm)²). Instead I run one BFS seeded with all the 1s at distance 0; BFS reaches each cell first from its nearest 1, so I fill the answer in O(nm) time and space."
Edge cases: Grid of all 1s (all zeros); a single 1 (BFS from one source); 1 x m or n x 1 grids.
Common mistakes: Running BFS from each 0 to find a 1 (O((nm)²) again); using 0 as "unvisited" in dist (conflicts with real distance 0).

Follow-ups: "Can you do it without a queue?" Two DP passes: top-left to bottom-right taking min from top/left, then bottom-right to top-left taking min from bottom/right. Same O(nm), O(1) extra. 10.17
simple: For every cell, find the distance to the nearest 1.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Compare every cell with every 1.
steps: Collect the coordinates of all 1 s.
For every cell, compute the minimum Manhattan distance to any 1.
approaches.why: Each of the n·m cells scans up to n·m ones; the list of ones and the output grid.
approaches.simple: For each cell, check the distance to every 1 and take the smallest.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Multi-source BFS from all 1 s.
steps: dist[r][c] = 0 for ones (push them), -1 for everything else (unvisited).
Pop a cell; for each neighbour with dist == -1, set dist = current + 1 and push.
Return dist.
approaches.why: Each cell is assigned and enqueued once.
approaches.simple: Multi-source BFS: start from all 1s together and spread outward one step at a time.

title: Number of distinct islands
problem: Given an m x n binary grid, count the number of distinct islands (4-directional). Two islands are the same if one can be translated (shifted, not rotated or reflected) to match the other. (LeetCode 694, premium; also on GFG.)
example: Explanation: The top-left "L" and the bottom-right "J" have different shapes; the top-right pair and bottom-
left pair are the same horizontal domino. So 3 distinct shapes.
intuition: We need a signature that is the same for identical shapes regardless of where they sit. Record each island cell relative to a fixed base cell: (r - baseR, c - baseC). If the base is always the island's first cell in row-major scan order (the cell where we start the DFS), then two islands with the same shape get exactly the same set of relative coordinates.

Even better, if the DFS always tries directions in the same order, identical shapes produce the relative coordinates in the same order, so you can just join them into a string and drop it into a HashSet. The answer is the set's size.
notes: Say it like this: "I need a translation-invariant signature for each island. I record each cell relative to the island's first cell in scan order and join them into a string in DFS order; identical shapes give identical strings, so a HashSet counts distinct shapes. That's O(mn) time and space, versus comparing every pair of shapes in the brute force."
Edge cases: No islands (0); all islands identical (1); single-cell islands all count as one shape.

Common mistakes: Storing absolute coordinates (no translation invariance); recording only the direction path without backtrack markers (two different shapes can give the same path string; relative coordinates avoid that problem); using a List<int[]> in a HashSet in Java (arrays use identity hashing, so nothing ever matches).

Follow-ups: "Rotations and reflections count as the same?" (LC 711) Generate all 8 transforms of the coordinates, normalize each (sort, shift to min), and take the lexicographically smallest as the canonical form. 10.18
simple: Count islands with different shapes (same shape moved around counts once).

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Collect normalized shapes and compare them pairwise. 1. For each island, collect relative coordinates, sort them.
steps: Compare the shape against every shape already stored (element by element). Store it if no match. 3. Answer = number of stored shapes.
approaches.time: O(k · m·n) for comparisons on top of O(m·n log(m·n)) sorting, where k is the number of islands (O((m·n)²) worst case)
approaches.why: Each new island is compared against all previous distinct shapes; total stored cells is at most m·n.
approaches.simple: Record each island's shape and compare it against every shape already saved.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Hash a canonical string per island.
steps: Scan in row-major order; for each new island start DFS with base = start cell.
DFS in a fixed direction order and append "dr,dc;" for each cell to a StringBuilder.
Add the string to a HashSet. Return the set size.
approaches.why: Each cell is visited once and contributes a constant-length piece to one signature; hashing the strings costs their total length, which is O(m·n).
approaches.simple: Record each island's cells relative to its first cell and put that shape in a set.

title: Detect a cycle in an undirected graph
problem: Given an undirected graph with V vertices (0..V-1) as an adjacency list adj, return true if it contains a cycle. The graph may be disconnected. (GFG signature: isCycle(int V, ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adj).)
intuition: In an undirected graph every edge appears in both directions, so when you go u → v, v 's list contains u again. That is not a cycle; it is the edge you just came along. So track the parent: while exploring v, ignore the neighbour equal to its parent.

If during traversal you meet a neighbour that is already visited and is not your parent, you reached it by a second path, which means a cycle. Run the traversal from every unvisited node to cover all components.
notes: Say it like this: "In an undirected graph I track each node's parent, because the edge back to the parent isn't a cycle. If I see an already-visited neighbour that isn't my parent, there's a second path, so a cycle. Brute force removes each edge and checks connectivity, O(E·(V+E)); DFS is O(V + E) time and O(V) space. Union-Find also works: an edge whose ends already share a root is a cycle."
Edge cases: Disconnected graph (loop over all nodes); isolated vertices; self-loop u–u (detected, since u is visited and u!= parent).

Common mistakes: Using the directed-graph method here (or vice versa); only starting DFS from node 0; with parallel edges u–v twice, the parent check by vertex hides the cycle; track the parent edge id if multi-edges are possible.
Follow-ups: "BFS version?" Queue stores (node, parent); same rule. "Return the cycle?" Keep a parent array and walk back from both endpoints when the cycle is found. 10.19
simple: Does an undirected graph contain a cycle?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: An edge (u, v) lies on a cycle exactly when u and v stay connected after removing that edge.
steps: For each edge u–v (handle each once, u < v), BFS from u while pretending that edge does not exist.
If v is still reachable, return true.
If no edge passes the test, return false.
approaches.why: One BFS per edge.
approaches.simple: For each edge, check whether its two ends are still connected without it.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: DFS with parent, over all components.
steps: visited[] all false.
For each unvisited node, dfs(node, -1).
In dfs(u, parent): mark u; for each neighbour v: if unvisited, recurse and propagate true; else if v!= parent, return true.
approaches.why: Every vertex is visited once and every adjacency entry checked once; visited array plus recursion stack.
approaches.simple: DFS while remembering where you came from. Meeting an already visited node that isn't your parent means a cycle.

title: Bipartite graph
problem: Given an undirected graph as an adjacency list graph (node i is adjacent to every node in graph[i]), return true if it is bipartite: its nodes can be split into two sets so that every edge joins a node from one set to a node from the other. The graph may be disconnected. (LeetCode 785.)
intuition: Bipartite = 2-colorable: color nodes red/blue so no edge has the same color on both ends. Try to color greedily: give a start node color 0; all its neighbours must be color 1; their neighbours must be color 0, and so on. There's no choice anywhere once the start is fixed, so if you ever find an edge whose ends already have the same color, it's impossible.
A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle, and this coloring detects one automatically. Remember to start a new BFS in every uncolored component.
notes: Say it like this: "Bipartite means 2-colorable. Brute force tries all 2^V colorings. But once one node's color is fixed, all its neighbours are forced, so a BFS that assigns opposite colors and checks for a same-colored edge decides it in O(V + E) time and O(V) space. It fails exactly when there's an odd cycle."
Edge cases: Disconnected graph (start BFS in every component); isolated nodes (fine); a graph with no edges (bipartite).
Common mistakes: Only BFS from node 0; using a boolean visited instead of a color array (you lose the information needed for the check).

Follow-ups: "DFS version?" Same rule recursively. "Possible Bipartition (LC 886)?" Build the graph from dislike pairs, then run this. "Union-Find?" Union all neighbours of u together; if u ends up with the same root as a neighbour, not bipartite. 10.20
simple: Can you colour the graph with two colours so every edge joins different colours?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Try every coloring.
steps: For each of the 2^V assignments of colors (bitmask), check every edge.
If some assignment has no same-colored edge, return true.
approaches.why: 2^V masks, each checking all edges. Only feasible for tiny V, but it shows what we're searching for.
approaches.simple: Try every possible colouring.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: BFS coloring per component.
steps: color[i] = -1 (uncolored).
For each uncolored node: color it 0 and BFS.
For each neighbour: if uncolored, give it the opposite color and enqueue; if it has the same color as the current node, return false.
Return true.
approaches.why: Each node is colored and enqueued once; each edge is checked twice.
approaches.simple: BFS and colour neighbours the opposite colour. If a neighbour already has your colour, it's impossible.

title: Detect a cycle in a directed graph
problem: Given a directed graph with V vertices (0..V-1) as an adjacency list adj, return true if it contains a cycle. (GFG signature: isCyclic(int V, ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adj).)
intuition: The undirected trick ("visited and not my parent") does not work for directed graphs. Example: 0 → 1, 0 → 2, 2 → 1. DFS visits 0, 1, then from 2 it sees 1 already visited. That's not a cycle; 1 was simply reached by two different paths.

A directed cycle exists only if you reach a node that is still on the current DFS path (an ancestor in the recursion). So keep two pieces of state: visited (ever seen) and onPath (in the current recursion stack). Equivalently, 3 colors: 0 = unvisited, 1 = on path, 2 = done. Seeing a color-1 node means a back edge, which means a cycle. When a node finishes, set it to 2 so it is never re-explored; anything reachable from a finished node is already known to be cycle-free.
notes: Say it like this: "In a directed graph a cycle means reaching a node that's still on my current DFS path, so I use three states: unvisited, on-path, done. Brute force checks from every node whether it can return to itself, O(V·(V+E)). The 3-state DFS is O(V + E) time, O(V) space. Kahn's algorithm is an equally good alternative: if the topological order has fewer than V nodes, there's a cycle."
Edge cases: Self-loops (cycle); disconnected graph; a DAG with diamond shapes (must NOT be reported as a cycle).
Common mistakes: Using the undirected "parent" rule; forgetting to reset/mark the node as done (state 2) on the way out, so it either stays "on path" (false positives) or gets re-explored (slow).

Follow-ups: "Iterative to avoid stack overflow?" Use Kahn's BFS. "Find all nodes not on or leading to a cycle?" That's Eventual Safe States (LC 802): exactly the nodes that end in state 2 without hitting a cycle, or Kahn's on the reversed graph. 10.21
simple: Does a directed graph contain a cycle?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Check, for each node, whether it can reach itself.
steps: For each node s, run a BFS starting from s 's neighbours with a fresh visited array.
If s is reached, there is a cycle through s: return true.
approaches.why: One full BFS per vertex.
approaches.simple: From each node, search to see if you can come back to it.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: 3-state DFS over all components.
steps: state[] = 0 for all.
For each node with state 0, run dfs.
dfs(u): state[u] = 1; for each v: if state[v] == 1 return true; if state[v] == 0 and dfs(v) is true, return true. Then state[u] = 2, return false.
approaches.why: Each node goes 0 → 1 → 2 once, and each edge is examined once; state array plus recursion stack.
approaches.simple: DFS with three states: unvisited, on the current path, finished. Reaching a node that is on the current path means a cycle.

title: Topological sort or Kahn's algorithm
pattern: Topological sort (DFS finish order / Kahn's BFS)
problem: Given a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with V vertices as an adjacency list adj, return any topological order: a list of all vertices such that for every edge u → v, u appears before v. (GFG signature: topoSort(int V, ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adj).)
example: Explanation: Every edge points left-to-right. Other orders like [5, 4, 2, 3, 1, 0] are also valid.
intuition: Two classic ways, both O(V + E). Know both.

Kahn's (BFS): a node with in-degree 0 has nothing that must come before it, so it can go first. Output it, "delete" its outgoing edges (decrement neighbours' in-degree), and repeat with any node that now has in-degree 0. A queue keeps track of the ready nodes.

DFS finish order: when DFS finishes a node u (all of its descendants are fully explored), every node that must come after u is already finished. So if you push nodes onto a stack at finish time, popping the stack gives a valid order (i.e. reverse finish order).
Kahn's has a bonus: if the output has fewer than V nodes, the graph had a cycle. That's why it doubles as directed cycle detection.
notes: Say it like this: "A topological order exists only for a DAG. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes in-degree-0 nodes using a queue; the DFS approach pushes nodes on a stack when they finish and reverses. Both are O(V + E) time and O(V) space; picking the ready node by scanning would be O(V²). Kahn's also tells me if there's a cycle, because then fewer than V nodes come out."
Edge cases: Disconnected DAG (start from every node / seed every in-degree-0 node); single node; multiple valid answers (judge accepts any).
Common mistakes: Adding the node to the DFS result before visiting children (that's preorder, not topological); forgetting to reverse; in Kahn's, computing in-degree on the wrong endpoint.

Follow-ups: "Alien Dictionary?" Build edges from the first differing letter of adjacent words, then topo sort. "Shortest path in a DAG with weights?" Relax edges in topological order, O(V + E). "Unique topological order?" It's unique iff the queue never holds more than one node. 10.22
simple: Order the nodes so every edge points forward.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Repeatedly scan for a node with in-degree
steps: Compute in-degrees.
V times: scan all vertices to find an unused one with in-degree 0; output it, mark used, decrement its neighbours.
approaches.why: Each of V rounds scans all V vertices; each edge is decremented once.
approaches.simple: Repeatedly scan for a node with no remaining incoming edges and take it.

approaches.label: Optimal (DFS + Stack)
steps: For each unvisited node, DFS.
After all neighbours of u are explored, push u onto a stack.
Pop everything from the stack: that is the topological order.
approaches.why: Each node and edge is processed once; visited array, stack and recursion depth are O(V).
approaches.simple: DFS; a node is added after all its descendants are done, and the reversed finish order is a valid order.

approaches.label: Optimal (Kahn's BFS)
steps: Compute in-degrees; queue every node with in-degree 0.
Pop u, append to answer, decrement each neighbour's in-degree, enqueue those that hit 0.
Answer has V nodes for a DAG (fewer ⇒ cycle).
approaches.why: Each node enters the queue once and each edge is relaxed once; in-degree array and queue are O(V).
approaches.simple: Kahn's BFS: queue nodes with no incoming edges, and remove their edges as you take them.

title: Kosaraju's algorithm
problem: Given a directed graph with V vertices as an adjacency list adj, return the number of strongly connected components (SCCs). An SCC is a maximal set of vertices where every vertex can reach every other vertex in the set. (GFG signature: kosaraju(int V, ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adj); some newer versions pass only adj and you take V = adj.size().)
intuition: Two vertices are in the same SCC exactly when each can reach the other. If you squash each SCC into one "super node", the result is a DAG. Kosaraju uses this structure in two passes:

1. Pass 1: Run DFS on the original graph and record vertices by finish time (push on a stack when done). The vertex finished last belongs to a "source" SCC of that DAG (nothing outside points into it from a later-finishing SCC). 2. Reverse all edges (transpose graph). The SCCs stay the same, but the DAG of SCCs flips direction, so that source SCC is now a sink: from it you can't escape to other SCCs. 3. Pass 2: Pop vertices from the stack (latest finish first). Each time you find an unvisited one, DFS on the transposed graph. That DFS stays trapped inside exactly one SCC. Count how many times you start a DFS.
In the example: finish order puts 0's SCC last; in the reversed graph starting from 0 you reach only {0,1,2} (the edge 0→3 now points 3→0, which you can't follow from 0).
notes: Say it like this: "SCCs are groups where everyone reaches everyone. Brute force builds the full reachability matrix, O(V·(V+E)) time and O(V²) space. Kosaraju does it in O(V + E): DFS once to get finish order, reverse the edges, then DFS on the reversed graph in decreasing finish time; each DFS in the second pass covers exactly one SCC."
Edge cases: DAG (every vertex is its own SCC, answer V); whole graph one cycle (answer 1); isolated vertices; self-loops (don't change the count).

Common mistakes: Doing pass 2 on the original graph instead of the transpose (DFS leaks into other SCCs); using the order from pass 1 in the wrong direction (must process the latest finished vertex first); forgetting to reset visited.

Follow-ups: "List the SCCs?" Collect vertices during each pass-2 DFS. "One pass?" Tarjan's algorithm uses discovery times and low-links with a single DFS and a stack; same O(V + E). "Condensation DAG?" Map each vertex to its SCC id and add edges between different ids. 10.23
simple: Count groups where every node can reach every other node (strongly connected components).

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Compute full reachability, then group mutually reachable pairs.
steps: For each vertex i, DFS to fill reach[i][*].
Walk the vertices; for each unassigned i, start a new SCC and assign every j with reach[i][j] && reach[j] [i].
Return the number of SCCs.
approaches.why: One DFS per vertex, plus the V × V reachability matrix and the grouping scan.
approaches.simple: Work out who can reach whom with a search from every node, then group mutual reachability.

approaches.why: Two DFS passes and one pass to build the transpose; the transpose graph needs O(V + E) memory.

title: Bridges in graph
problem: Given n servers (0..n-1) and undirected connections, a critical connection (bridge) is an edge whose removal disconnects some servers from others. Return all bridges in any order. (LeetCode 1192 "Critical Connections in a Network"; the graph is connected and has no duplicate edges.)
example: Explanation: 0-1-2 form a cycle, so none of those edges is critical. Removing 1-3 isolates node 3.
intuition: An edge is a bridge if it is not on any cycle. Detecting that for all edges at once uses two numbers per vertex during a DFS:

tin[u]: the time (counter) when DFS first reached u. low[u]: the smallest tin reachable from u 's DFS subtree using tree edges downwards plus at most one back edge (an edge to an already-visited vertex other than the parent).

Now look at a tree edge u → v (v is u's child). If low[v] > tin[u], then nothing in v 's subtree can reach u or anything above it without using the edge u–v itself. Remove that edge and the subtree is cut off: it is a bridge. If low[v] <= tin[u], some back edge goes around it, so it's on a cycle.

Trace on the example (start at 0): tin 0=0, 1=1, 2=2. From 2, neighbour 0 is visited (not parent) → low[2] = 0. Back at 1: low[1] = min(1, 0) = 0. Then 3: tin 3=3, no other neighbours, low[3] = 3. Edge 1–3: low[3]=3 > tin[1]=1 → bridge. Edge 1–2: low[2]=0 ≤ 1 → not a bridge.
notes: Say it like this: "A bridge is an edge on no cycle. Removing each edge and running BFS is O(E·(V+E)). Tarjan's algorithm does one DFS keeping discovery time and low-link, the earliest discovery time a subtree can reach with one back edge. For a tree edge u→v, if low[v] > tin[u], v's subtree can't reach u without that edge, so it's a bridge. O(V + E) time and space."
Edge cases: Tree graph (every edge is a bridge); single cycle (no bridges); disconnected graph (loop over all vertices).

Common mistakes: Using >= instead of > (that's the articulation point condition); updating low[u] with low[v] for a back edge instead of tin[v]; skipping the parent by vertex when parallel edges exist (then skip by edge id instead). On LeetCode with n up to 10^5, deep recursion can overflow in some languages; an iterative DFS fixes it.

Follow-ups: "Articulation points?" Same DFS, condition low[v] >= tin[u] plus a special root rule (next question). "2-edge-connected components?" Remove the bridges; the remaining connected components are the answer. 10.24
simple: Find every edge whose removal disconnects the graph.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Remove each edge and test connectivity.
steps: Build the adjacency list storing edge ids.
For each edge i = (u, v): BFS from u ignoring edge i. If v is not reached, edge i is a bridge.
approaches.why: One BFS per edge.
approaches.simple: Remove each edge and check if the graph is still connected.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Tarjan's bridge-finding DFS.
steps: tin[] = -1, low[], timer = 0.

dfs(u, parent): tin[u] = low[u] = timer++. For each neighbour v other than parent: - unvisited: dfs(v, u), then low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); if low[v] > tin[u], record bridge [u, v]. - visited: back edge, low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v]).
Call dfs from every unvisited vertex.
approaches.why: One DFS visits each vertex and edge once; adjacency list, the two arrays and recursion stack.
approaches.simple: Tarjan: record when each node is first reached and the earliest time reachable from below it. If a child can't reach above its parent, that edge is a bridge.

title: Articulation point in graph
problem: Given an undirected graph with V vertices as an adjacency list adj, return all articulation points (cut vertices) in sorted order: vertices whose removal (with their edges) increases the number of connected components. If there are none, return [-1]. (GFG signature: articulationPoints(int V, ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adj).)
example: Explanation: Removing 1 cuts off 0. Removing 4 separates {0,1} from {2,3}.
intuition: Same tin / low DFS as bridges, but now we ask about vertices.

For a non-root vertex u with DFS child v: if low[v] >= tin[u], then v 's subtree cannot reach anything above u without passing through u. Removing u cuts that subtree off, so u is an articulation point. Note >= (not > as for bridges): the subtree reaching u itself is fine for an edge, but here u is the thing being removed, so reaching u doesn't help.

The root of the DFS tree has nothing above it, so the rule changes: the root is an articulation point iff it has more than one DFS child. Two DFS children of the root can only be connected through the root (otherwise DFS would have found the second one from inside the first subtree).
Also unlike bridges, for a back edge we still use low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v]); using low[v] there would be wrong.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force deletes each vertex and counts components, O(V·(V+E)). Tarjan's algorithm does one DFS with discovery times and low-links: a non-root u is a cut vertex if some child v has low[v] >= tin[u], meaning v's subtree can't reach above u without u; the root is a cut vertex only if it has more than one DFS child. That's O(V + E) time, O(V) space."

Edge cases: No articulation points (return [-1]); disconnected graph (each component's DFS root gets the root rule); a star graph (only the centre); a single edge 0–1 (no cut vertices, the root has one child).

Common mistakes: Applying the low[v] >= tin[u] rule to the root (every root would be marked); using > (bridge condition) instead of >=; using low[v] for back edges; adding u to the result list multiple times (use a boolean array).
Follow-ups: "Bridges instead?" Same DFS with low[v] > tin[u] and no root rule. "Biconnected components?" Keep a stack of edges during the DFS and pop a component whenever low[v] >= tin[u].
simple: Find every node whose removal disconnects the graph.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Remove each vertex and count components.
steps: Count connected components of the full graph: base.
For each vertex x: count components of the graph with x deleted. If that count is greater than base, x is an articulation point.
Return the sorted list, or [-1] if empty.
approaches.why: One full traversal per removed vertex. (Removing an isolated vertex lowers the count by 1, so > base is the correct test.)
approaches.simple: Remove each node and count connected pieces.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Tarjan's articulation-point DFS.
steps: tin[] = -1, low[], timer = 0, isAP[].

dfs(u, parent): tin[u] = low[u] = timer++, children = 0. For each neighbour v!= parent: - unvisited: dfs(v, u), low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); if parent!= -1 && low[v] >= tin[u], mark u; children++. - visited: low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v]). After the loop, if parent == -1 && children > 1, mark u.
Run from every unvisited vertex; collect marked vertices in increasing order (or [-1]).
approaches.why: One DFS over all vertices and edges; the arrays and recursion stack are O(V). (A vertex can satisfy the condition for several children, which is why we use a boolean array instead of adding to a list directly.)
approaches.simple: Tarjan with discovery and low times: a node is critical if some child can't reach above it (the root needs two or more children).
